title: Praying with the qazi
hook: tradition says that at prayer he told the qazi his mind had wandered home to a young horse
carry: where is your mind right now

segments.voice: Yesterday: the first words after. There is no Hindu, there is no Muslim. Your line was beneath the labels, people. Which label did you set aside? Day thirty.
screen: `THE FIRST WORDS AFTER — BENEATH THE LABELS, PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: You're standing in a place of worship. The words are familiar, you've said them a thousand times, and your body knows exactly when to stand, when to bow. And your mind? Your mind is in the parking lot. Did I lock the car? It's in tomorrow's meeting. It's replaying an argument from last week. Anyone who has ever prayed, meditated or even tried to listen to a friend knows this. The body shows up. The mind wanders off. Five hundred years ago in Sultanpur, the story goes, a religious judge had exactly that happen to him, at exactly the wrong moment, standing next to exactly the wrong person. Today, praying with the qazi.
screen: `THE BODY KNOWS WHEN TO BOW.` → `THE MIND IS IN THE PARKING LOT.` → `SULTANPUR, AT PRAYER.`

segments.voice: Here's the story as the janamsakhis tell it. Word of Nanak's sentence reached the governor, Daulat Khan, and the town's qazi, the Muslim judge. They called him in. If there is no Hindu and no Muslim, they said, then come and pray with us. It was Friday. Nanak went with them to the mosque. The prayer began. The governor and the qazi bowed. And Nanak stood there, quietly, and didn't join in. Afterward the qazi was indignant. You came to pray with us, and you didn't pray. And Nanak, the story says, answered gently: who was I supposed to pray with? The governor's mind, he said, was far away in Kabul, buying horses. And the qazi's mind was at home, where a mare had just given birth, worrying that the young foal might wander off and fall into the open well in the courtyard. The story says both men were silent, because it was true. Now, it's important to hear what this story isn't. It isn't mocking Muslim prayer, or any prayer. Muslim teachers themselves have long stressed that prayer needs a present heart, humble attention; there's a word for it in Arabic, khushu. Nanak's point sits right beside theirs. Tradition connects the moment with a hymn of Nanak's, in the scripture, about what makes a true Muslim. In paraphrase: let mercy be your mosque, faith your prayer mat, honest living your holy book. His challenge was never to stop praying. It was to actually be there when you do. Which is exactly why the story is so uncomfortable. Every one of us has been the qazi, standing in the right place with our mind at home by the well.
screen: `THEN COME AND PRAY WITH US.` · `THE MIND IN KABUL. THE MIND BY THE WELL.` · `NOT MOCKERY. A PRESENT HEART.` · `LET MERCY BE YOUR MOSQUE.` · then, large: `WHERE IS YOUR MIND RIGHT NOW?`

segments.voice: Let's try giving one thing your whole mind. If you pray, choose one short prayer you know, from your own tradition, and say it slowly, meaning every word. If you don't, choose one simple thing: your breath, or a single sound in the room. Each time your mind wanders off to the car, the meeting, the well, notice where it went, and gently bring it back. No scolding. Just come back. The bell holds the time.
Praying with the qazi. Nanak stands at prayer and sees that the minds beside him have wandered off to horses and a foal by the well.
Your line: where is your mind right now. Ask it three times today, in the middle of doing something, and bring your mind back to where your body is. Day thirty.

howItsDone: Sikhs tell the story of Guru Nanak and the qazi as a sakhi about attention in prayer, and link it with his hymns on what gives worship its meaning.

fork.setup: you're Nanak at Friday prayer. the governor and the qazi are bowing, but you can see their minds are elsewhere. what do you do?
options: bow along with them so nobody's offended.
stand quietly, and afterward tell them gently where their minds were.
fork.reveal: the story says he stood, and afterward asked: who was I to pray with? one mind was in Kabul, the other by the well.

original.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi script: qazi, a Muslim judge; the word comes from Arabic.

trapdoor: what you thought: Nanak refused to pray with Muslims.
what it means: he went to pray with them, and showed that a prayer with the mind elsewhere is hardly a prayer at all.
what a scholar hears: tradition links the story with Nanak's hymn in Var Majh on the true Muslim: mercy for a mosque, faith for a prayer mat, honest living for scripture.
